'''''Melaleuca decussata''''', commonly known as '''cross-leaf honey-myrtle''' or '''totem poles''', is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Myrtaceae]] native to [[South Australia]] and both native and naturalised in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]]. It is an adaptable shrub, grown in many parts of [[Australia]] for its attractive foliage but it is regarded as an environmental weed in parts of Victoria.

==Description==
''Melaleuca decussata'' is a densely branched shrub growing to a height and width of {{convert|3|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}}. The leaves are arranged in alternating pairs at right angles to the ones above and below so that the leaves are in 4 rows along the stems ([[Phyllotaxy|decussate]]). The leaves are {{convert|4.5-15|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|0.5-3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide, linear, narrowly elliptic or narrow egg-shaped tapering to a point and concave in cross section. They also have prominent oil glands on their lower surface.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|page=141|location=Canberra|isbn=9781922137517}}</ref><ref name=Holliday>{{cite book|last1=Holliday|first1=Ivan|title=Melaleucas : a field and garden guide|date=2004|publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers|location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W.|isbn=1876334983|pages=84–85|edition=2nd}}</ref>

The flowers are a shade of pink or purple but fade rapidly to white. They are arranged in spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering and on the sides of the branches. The spikes are up to {{convert|16|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter, {{convert|20-30|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and have between 6 and 22 individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|1.8-2.3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower ages. The stamens are arranged in five bundles around the flowers with 12 to 26 stamens in each bundle. The flowering season is from August to May but flowers mostly appear from November to February in the species' native range.  The fruit which follows are woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]], characteristically fused together at their bases and sunken in the stem.<ref name=Brophy/><ref name=Holliday/><ref name=Viridans>{{cite book |title=Wild Plants of Victoria (database)|year=2009 |publisher=Viridans Biological Databases & Department of Sustainability and Environment}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca decussata'' was first formally described by [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in 1812 in the second edition of ''[[Hortus Kewensis]]'' from material collected from the southern coastal region of Australia.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca decussata''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/510522|publisher=APNI|accessdate=3 May 2015}}</ref><ref name=Hortus>{{cite book|last1=Aiton|first1=William|title=Hortus Kewensis Edition 2, Volume 4|date=1812|location=London|page=415|url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/ing/Libro.php?Libro=3050|accessdate=3 May 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''decussata'') refers to the decussate arrangement of the leaves.<ref name=Brophy/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Melaleuca decussata'' occurs between coastal areas of South Australia (including the [[Eyre Peninsula]]) and the centre of eastern Victoria.<ref name=Brophy/>
[[File:Melaleuca decussata 2.JPG|thumb|225px|Fruit sunken in stem]]

==Conservation status==
This species has been declared an environmental weed in the [[Geelong]] area, the catchments of the [[Broken River (Victoria)|Broken]] and [[Goulburn River|Goulburn]] rivers and the [[Wimmera]] bioregion. It is a garden escape which becomes naturalised in grasslands and grassy woodland. It is believed to be a threat to several natural vegetation associations and forms dense stands in native pastures.<ref name=weeds>{{cite web|title=Cross-leaved honey-myrtle|url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/melaleuca_decussata.htm|publisher=Queensland government:Weeds of Australia|accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref> It grows in low nutrient soils subject to inundation.<ref name=Viridans/>

==Use in horticulture==
''Melaleuca decussata'' is a hardy garden plant with attractive foliage. It will grow in most situations and has attractive mauve-coloured flowers, although they fade quickly to white.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0002165759|page=262|edition=2nd}}</ref> It is not advisable to plant this species within {{convert|6|m|ft|sigfig=1}} of a wastewater pipe because of its potential to cause damage.<ref name=water>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca decussata''|url=http://www.sydneywater.com.au/SW/your-home/saving-water-at-home/garden-and-pool/plant-selector/plant-detail/SWP_CDF_DD_050814|publisher=Sydney Water|accessdate=3 May 2015}}</ref>
